Yesterday we learned that a judge allowed a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed accusing Apple's Photos app facial recognition feature of violating state privacy laws.

The case is being conflated with how Meta uses facial recognition, even though the two companies sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum. The court's decision to let it proceed shows a fundamental misunderstanding of how the feature works...

The earlier lawsuit against Meta

To properly understand the current situation, we need to revisit a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta, which dates back to 2015.

Because the facial recognition was performed on Meta's servers, and Meta was able to identify the faces, the company did break the law, and was ultimately forced to settle for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA), which requires companies to obtain consent before collecting biometric data.

Apple's approach is completely different

Here's the major problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect any biometric data when it performs facial recognition in the Photos app. As Apple explained in a machine learning research paper published in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Not only that, but the iPhone only determines "these photos appear to be of the same person" — it has no idea who that person actually is. Only the iPhone user can attach a name label to that person.

Apple's Photos privacy policy corroborates this.

Remarkably, this lawsuit has now entered its sixth year in the legal system, and a few minutes of research shows its allegations simply do not hold up.

Courts and legislatures should be actively celebrating Apple's approach to privacy, not conflating it with the privacy-violating practices of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislatures fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example is, of course, end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, while being completely ignorant of how it actually works.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every field they need to venture into. But they do have access to experts — what I find baffling is that such lawsuits and legislative drafts can progress for years without anyone pointing out such a fundamental flaw.
